words.connector: Think of Snapshot Isolation like reading yesterday's newspaper while the live broadcast continues: your view of the world is consistent and complete as of when you sat down, even if major events are happening right now — you just don't see them until you pick up tomorrow's paper.
words.techContext: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ isolation level implements Snapshot Isolation via its MVCC engine; each transaction's snapshot is taken at the first query of the transaction and held for its duration.
words.exampleSentence: The monthly report query ran for 8 minutes under Snapshot Isolation without blocking any concurrent writes, because MVCC gave it a fixed snapshot at the start of the transaction while the OLTP load continued writing new rows unobstructed.
words.etymology: Snapshot from the photographic snapshot metaphor — the database state is 'photographed' at the start of the transaction; Isolation from the ACID isolation property. Formalized by Berenson et al. in their 1995 SIGMOD critique of SQL isolation levels.

words.shortDefinition: A concurrency anomaly where two transactions read overlapping data and each writes based on the other's pre-change view.
words.simpleDefinition: Write skew is the concurrency anomaly that Snapshot Isolation fails to prevent. Two concurrent transactions T1 and T2 each read the same data, make decisions based on what they see, and each writes to a different row — so there is no write-write conflict to detect. But their combined result violates an application invariant that neither transaction violated individually. The classic example: two doctors both check 'at least one doctor on call?' and both go off-call simultaneously, leaving nobody on duty.
words.longDefinition: Write skew arises in Snapshot Isolation when two transactions have anti-dependency cycles: T1 reads data later written by T2, and T2 reads data later written by T1. Because neither transaction writes to the row the other has written (no write-write conflict), SI's first-committer-wins rule does not abort either transaction. The combined result is anomalous. The canonical example from Berenson et al.: a hospital database with an invariant 'at least one doctor must be on call'. T1 reads: two doctors on call — checks out; writes: doctor Alice off-call. T2 reads: two doctors on call — checks out; writes: doctor Bob off-call. Both commit under SI. Result: no doctors on call, invariant violated. Write skew can occur whenever an application reads a set of rows, computes a decision, and writes to a row in that set (or a row related to it) based on the decision. Prevention options: (1) Serializable isolation (full serializability prevents write skew by definition); (2) Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) in PostgreSQL detects anti-dependency cycles and aborts one transaction; (3) Explicit locking — SELECT FOR UPDATE on the rows read forces T2 to block until T1 commits, serializing the critical section. The phantoms variant (new rows inserted satisfying the read predicate) is the phantom read anomaly.
words.connector: Think of write skew like two roommates both checking the fridge ('is there enough food for a party?'), both seeing a full fridge and each inviting 20 people, while neither buys more food — the combined effect violates the 'enough food' invariant even though neither individual decision was wrong at the time.
words.techContext: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ (Snapshot Isolation) is vulnerable to write skew; use SERIALIZABLE isolation or SELECT FOR UPDATE to prevent it in critical sections.
words.exampleSentence: The double-booking bug was a textbook write skew: both reservation transactions read 'one seat remaining' under Snapshot Isolation, both wrote a booking for that seat, and neither saw a conflict because they wrote to different booking_id rows.
words.etymology: Write skew named for the 'skewed' (asymmetric) nature of the conflict: two transactions read the same data but write to different parts of it, so the conflict is not a direct write-write collision. Formalized by Berenson et al. in their 1995 SIGMOD paper.

words.shortDefinition: Buffer pool eviction policy: evict the page not accessed for the longest time; most common approximation in production.
words.simpleDefinition: LRU (Least Recently Used) replacement evicts the buffer pool frame whose page has not been accessed for the longest time when a new page must be loaded and no free frames are available. The assumption is that recently accessed pages are more likely to be accessed again soon (temporal locality). True LRU requires tracking the exact last-access time of every page, which is expensive; production databases use approximations like the Clock algorithm or LRU-K.
words.longDefinition: The buffer pool manager must choose a victim frame to evict whenever a new page is needed and no free frame is available. LRU (Least Recently Used) is the theoretically optimal online eviction policy under workloads with strong temporal locality — accessing a page recently predicts accessing it again soon. In a pure LRU implementation, every page access updates a 'last used' timestamp (or moves the page to the front of an LRU list), and eviction always picks the tail. In practice, maintaining a precise LRU list is expensive under concurrent access (every read requires a write to the LRU structure). Production databases use approximations. The Clock algorithm ('Second Chance') gives each frame a reference bit: on access, set the bit; eviction sweeps the clock hand, clearing bits and evicting the first frame with a cleared bit. InnoDB uses LRU-K (specifically LRU-2): a page must be accessed at least twice before entering the 'hot' portion of the LRU list, protecting against large scans that would flush the entire buffer pool (the 'sequential flood' problem). PostgreSQL uses a Clock algorithm for shared_buffers. All LRU variants struggle with sequential scans: a full table scan accesses every page exactly once, polluting the buffer pool with pages that will never be re-accessed. InnoDB's two-list approach (young/old) mitigates this by initially placing scan pages in the 'old' list where they age out quickly without displacing frequently-used pages.
words.connector: Think of LRU replacement like a desk with limited space: when it fills up, you remove the book you haven't opened in the longest time. If you're reading the same reference books repeatedly, they stay; the ones gathering dust get put back on the shelf.
words.techContext: InnoDB uses a modified LRU with a young/old split (default 37% old): newly loaded pages enter the old portion and are promoted to young only after a second access within innodb_old_blocks_time (default 1000ms), protecting hot pages from scan pollution.
words.exampleSentence: The nightly full-table ETL scan evicted the entire working set of hot OLTP pages from the buffer pool, causing a 10-minute latency spike at the start of the morning trading session while the frequently-accessed index pages were re-read from disk.
words.etymology: LRU stands for Least Recently Used; the eviction policy was introduced in the virtual memory management literature of the 1960s and adopted for database buffer management. The Clock approximation was developed simultaneously in the OS and database communities.

words.shortDefinition: SSI: detects and aborts transactions whose snapshot-based execution would form a serialization anomaly cycle.
words.simpleDefinition: Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) upgrades Snapshot Isolation to full serializability by detecting dangerous concurrency patterns at runtime. SSI tracks anti-dependency edges — 'T1 read a value later written by T2' — and detects when these edges form a cycle in the transaction dependency graph (a serialization anomaly). When a dangerous cycle is detected, one of the involved transactions is aborted with a serialization error. SSI is the isolation algorithm behind PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level since version 9.1.
words.longDefinition: Michael Cahill, Uwe Röhm, and Alan Fekete introduced SSI in their 2008 SIGMOD paper 'Serializable Isolation for Snapshot Databases'. The key insight is that write skew and phantom anomalies under Snapshot Isolation always manifest as a specific cycle pattern in the transaction dependency graph: a 'dangerous structure' consisting of two consecutive rw-anti-dependency edges (T1 →rw T2 →rw T3 where T1 and T3 may be the same transaction). SSI instruments each transaction to track SIREAD locks (not blocking locks — just tracking what each transaction has read) and detects when incoming rw-anti-dependencies form dangerous structures. When a dangerous structure is detected, one of the involved transactions is aborted (the one that has not yet committed if possible). SSI is optimistic: it allows transactions to proceed concurrently and only aborts when an actual conflict is detected. The false abort rate (aborting transactions that would have been serializable) is low in practice. PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level implements SSI with per-predicate SIREAD locks; the pg_stat_activity view exposes SSI-related statistics. SSI is theoretically superior to Strict 2PL for read-heavy workloads because readers do not block writers, but it requires abort handling in application code and carries higher overhead for write-skew-prone workloads.
words.connector: Think of SSI like a traffic intersection with a smart camera instead of a traffic light: vehicles proceed freely and the camera watches for dangerous crossing patterns. When it detects a collision about to happen, it radios one car to stop — only those in a genuinely dangerous pattern are interrupted.
words.techContext: PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level uses SSI since version 9.1; SET default_transaction_isolation = 'serializable' enables it globally. The serialization_failures counter in pg_stat_database tracks how often SSI aborts transactions.
words.exampleSentence: After upgrading the bank's transfer service to PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE isolation, the write skew bug that allowed double-spending disappeared without any explicit SELECT FOR UPDATE locking, because SSI detected the anti-dependency cycle and aborted one of the two conflicting transactions.
words.etymology: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: Serializable (equivalent to serial execution) + Snapshot Isolation (the underlying concurrency mechanism). Coined by Cahill, Röhm, and Fekete in their 2008 SIGMOD paper.
